overview.body:
**Nagoya** ​(*nagoya*) — ‌Industrial ‌Hub, Chūbu ​· Peaceful ​ancient ​house — ​belongs ​to the ‌Japanese tradition, ​where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Industrial ​Hub, ‌Chūbu". The ​name ​means "Peaceful ​ancient house"[^1].

​**Nagoya** ​is Japan's ‌fourth-largest ​city and ‌a ​historic center ‌of commerce ​and ‌craftsmanship. Built ​around ‌the castle ​commissioned by ​Tokugawa ‌Ieyasu in ‌1610, ‌Nagoya grew ​into a ​hub ‌of ceramics, ​textiles, ​automotive manufacturing, ‌and trade. ​Its ​name — ‌'peaceful ​ancient house' ‌— ​reflects a ​city that ​has ​long served ‌as ‌a stable ​crossroads.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the name ​as ‌**Nagoya** and ‌serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/nagoya/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *nagoya* ​survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Japanese ​characters ​as ​**名古屋**. ​Etymologically ‌it means ​"Peaceful ​ancient ‌house"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII ​form *nagoya* ‌survives ​only ​because ​the ​early ​domain-name system ‌could ​not ‌carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a ‌technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ​ancient spelling. ‌The ‌Unicode ‌restoration ​**Nagoya** ​recovers ‌the full ​diacritic ​detail ‌of ​the ​scholarly ‌transliteration directly ​in ‌the ​address ​bar. ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form ‌— ​a ‌description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed ‌form ‌itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**n** ​→ ​**N** ‌— ​Same
- **a** ​→ ​**a** ‌— ​Same
- ​**g** ​→ **g** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**o** ​→ ‌**o** ​— Same
- ‌**y** ‌→ ​**y** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: The Cambridge History of Japan, vol. 4: Early Modern Japan (Cambridge, 1991).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/na.ɡo.ja/** ​— Modern ​Standard Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme by ‌phoneme:

- **Na-** ​— ​Alveolar nasal ‌[n] plus ​open ‌central [a]
- ​**-go-** — ‌Voiced ​velar stop ​[ɡ] plus ​open-mid [o]
- ​**-ya** ​— Palatal ‌approximant [j] ​plus ‌open central ​[a]

For ‌the ​modern speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation ‌is: 'NAH-goh-yah' ​— three ​even syllables, ‌with ‌the middle ‌vowel open ​and ​short.

Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ​of the ‌name:

- **Japanese** ​— ​名古屋 (Nagoya), ‌traditionally glossed ​'peaceful ancient ‌house' ​— a ​folk etymology ​the ​city wears ‌proudly
- **Castle** ‌— ​Nagoya-jō, the ‌Tokugawa fortress ​and ​city symbol
- ‌**Region** — ‌Aichi Prefecture, ‌Chūbu ‌region

Nagoya ​keeps its ‌restoration ​plain: plain ​Hepburn romanisation ​— ‌no diacritic, ​no distinctive ​letter; ​the restoration ‌marks the ​name as ​a ​proper noun. ‌The gloss ​'peaceful ‌ancient house' ​is a ‌folk ​etymology that ‌historians treat ‌with ​caution, but ​it is ​the meaning ​the ‌city itself ‌has always ​preferred.

sources.citation: The Cambridge History of Japan, vol. 4: Early Modern Japan (Cambridge, 1991).

domains.body:
**Nagoya** ​is Japan's ‌fourth-largest ‌city and ​a ​historic center ​of commerce ​and ​craftsmanship. Built ‌around ​the castle ​commissioned ‌by Tokugawa ​Ieyasu ‌in 1610, ​Nagoya ‌grew into ​a hub ​of ​ceramics, textiles, ​automotive ​manufacturing, and ‌trade. ​Its name ‌— ​'peaceful ancient ‌house' ​— reflects ‌a city ​that ‌has long ​served ​as a ‌stable ‌crossroads.[^1]

### Nagoya ‌Castle

​The Tokugawa ​fortress ‌ordered by ​Ieyasu in ​1610 ‌and completed ​in ​1612, crowned ‌by ​the famous ‌golden ​shachihoko roof ​ornaments.

### ​Industrial Hub

​From cotton ‌weaving ‌to the ​Toyota ‌Motor Corporation, ​the ​Chūkyō zone ‌became ‌one of ‌the ‌three engines ​of Japanese ‌manufacturing.

### ​Culinary Capital

​Famous ​for miso-katsu, ‌tebasaki, ​kishimen, and ​the ​beloved 'morning' ‌coffee ​custom that ​arrives with ​toast ‌and egg.

### ​Chūbu ‌Gateway

A ​strategic ‌point on ​the ‌Tōkaidō linking ‌eastern ​and western ​Japan — ​the ​reason the ‌castle ‌exists at ​all.

sources.citation: Totman, Conrad, Tokugawa Ieyasu: Shogun (Heian, 1983).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with Nagoya ‌concentrates ​in a ​small ​set of ​recurring attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- **Shachihoko** ​— The ‌golden ​tiger-headed carp ‌roof ​ornaments of ​Nagoya Castle ​— ​water beasts ​pressed into ‌service ​as fire ‌insurance, and ​the ‌city's emblem ​on ‌everything from ​manhole covers ‌to ​baseball caps.
- ​**Nagoya Castle ‌keep** ‌— The ‌fortress that ​was ​never attacked ‌in ​war: a ​1612 message ‌in ​stone, a ​1959 concrete ‌reconstruction, ​and since ‌2018 a ​document-faithful ​wooden Honmaru ​Palace ​rebuilt beside ‌it.
- **Red ‌miso ​(aka-dashi)** — ‌The dark, ​salty ​miso paste ‌of the ‌region, ‌central to ‌miso-katsu, ​miso-nikomi udon, ‌and the ​local ​conviction that ​flavor should ‌be ​deep rather ​than showy.
- ​**Ceramics ‌and cloisonné** ​— ​The long ​craft tradition ‌of ​the Seto–Nagoya ‌region — ​Noritake ‌porcelain, Shippo-yaki ​cloisonné, and ‌the ‌Owari guild ​instincts ​that made ​'made in ​Nagoya' ‌a quiet ‌synonym for ​quality.

sources.citation: The Cambridge History of Japan, vol. 4: Early Modern Japan (Cambridge, 1991).

mythology.body:
Nagoya's mythology is more ​historical than divine: a crossroads named for a ‌'peaceful ancient house,' a castle built to end ‌the age of war, a conference that ​settled Japan's succession, and a merchant city that ​traded the sword for the loom and then ​for the assembly line.[^1]

### The Peaceful Ancient ​House (Name origin)

The name is older than ​the castle, and its meaning is a folk ‌etymology the city wears proudly. 名古屋 is ​traditionally read 'peaceful ancient house' — na from ​名, 'name, famous,' goya a softened form of ‌koya, 'old house' — explained by the ​Nagoya Shrine, an old Owari sanctuary whose grounds ‌lay within what became the castle town. Historians ​treat the derivation with caution: the same ‌syllables appear in several Owari place names, and ​medieval documents already know 'Nagoya' as an ordinary ​locality, not a poetic one. But the ​etymology's modesty suits the city it names — ​neither Kyoto's courtly antiquity nor Edo's martial swagger, ​but a prosperous, unpretentious middle. The temple's ‌framing turns the question around: a 'peaceful ancient ​house' is precisely what a castle town promises ‌its merchants — safety, continuity, and a ​roof that outlasts the swords.[^2]

### The Building of ‌Nagoya Castle (Edo period)

After Sekigahara (1600) gave ​Tokugawa Ieyasu the country, he turned to ‌securing its spine. In 1610 he ordered a ​great castle raised at Nagoya — a site ‌no Japanese ruler had ever fortified — ​to command the Tōkaidō highways where eastern and ​western Japan meet, and to house his ninth ‌son, Yoshinao, as founder of the Owari ‌branch. Stone and timbers were floated down from ‌Sunpu and hauled over from the dismantled Kiyosu ​castle upstream; the great keep was complete ​by 1612, and Yoshinao entered as first lord ‌of Owari in 1616. The keep's roof carried the ​city's enduring emblem: a pair of golden ​shachihoko — tiger-headed carp, water beasts that guard ‌against fire — whose shine announced that this ​was Tokugawa work. The castle was never ​attacked in war. Its whole career is the ‌message it was built to send: the new ​shogunate could raise an unneeded fortress at the ‌center of the country and call it ​peace.

### The Kiyosu Conference (Sengoku)

Fourteen kilometers up ​the river stands Kiyosu, the older castle that ​ruled Owari before Nagoya existed, and the ​stage for one of the hinges of Japanese ‌history. In June 1582, weeks after Akechi Mitsuhide ‌burned Oda Nobunaga at Honnō-ji, the Oda ​retainers assembled at Kiyosu to decide who would ‌inherit a conquest half-made. The real contest was ​between Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Shibata Katsuie; it ​was settled in favor of Nobunaga's infant grandson ‌Hidenobu — and, in practice, in Hideyoshi's favor, ‌since the settlement freed him to finish ‌the unification and take the title of kampaku. ‌The chronicle tradition and the Cambridge History of ​Japan both mark the conference as the ‌turn between the age of warlords and the ​age of unification. Nagoya's story begins, in a ​sense, at that table: the castle Ieyasu ​would raise downstream in 1610 was the architectural ‌afterthought of decisions taken at Kiyosu in 1582.

### From ​Castle Town to Industrial City (Modern era)

​The samurai city became a merchant city almost ​as soon as the swords were put away. ‌With the Meiji abolition of the domains ​in 1871, the Owari warriors' stipends dissolved into ​commerce, and Nagoya's location — the rail junction ​of the Tōkaidō and the sea-lanes of ‌Ise Bay — made it the natural entrepôt ​of the Chūbu region; municipal status came in 1889. ‌The city industrialized along its oldest craft ​instincts: cotton and wool weaving first, then, with ‌the founding of Toyota in 1937, automobiles, so ​that the Chūkyō industrial zone became one ‌of the three engines of Japanese manufacturing. The ‌war found the city: the air raids of ​1945 burned the castle keep, and the ​concrete tower that replaced it in 1959 has ​only recently begun giving way to a wooden, ​document-faithful reconstruction of the lost Honmaru Palace, ‌opened in 2018. The 'peaceful ancient house,' bombed, burned, ‌and rebuilt twice in a century, keeps the ​bargain of its name.

sources.citation: Totman, Conrad, Tokugawa Ieyasu: Shogun (Heian, 1983).
Berry, Mary Elizabeth, Hideyoshi (Harvard, 1982).

syncretism.body:
Nagoya's ​identity is ‌a three-layer ‌alloy. The ​first ​layer is ​samurai: the ​Owari Tokugawa, ​the ‌'senior branch' ​(gosanke) held ​in ‌reserve to ​supply a ‌shogun should ​the ‌main line ​fail, cultivated ​a deliberate ​persona ​of *shitsujitsu ​gōken* — ‌sober, sturdy, ​unshowy ‌— to ​reassure the ‌shogunate and ​everyone ‌else. The ​second layer ‌is merchant: ​with ​the stipends ‌gone, the ‌castle ‌town's energies ​flowed into ​the *chōnindō*, ‌the ​way of ​the townsman, ‌whose creed ​of ​thrift, calculation, ‌and craft ​made Nagoya ‌famous ​for quality ​rather than ​fashion. The ​third ‌layer is ‌industrial: Toyota ​and its ‌satellites ​made the ​region synonymous ‌with ‌Japanese manufacturing ‌and its ‌methods. A ​city ‌that began ​as a ​political message ​became ‌an economic ​one; the ​shachihoko on ​the ‌keep now ​watch over ​a supply ​chain.[^1]

‌Kindred figures ​in the ‌PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index ‌include [[delphoi|Delphoí]], ​[[fuji|Fuji]], [[ise|Ise]], ‌[[kumano|Kumano]], ‌[[omphalos|Omphalós]], and ​[[shikoku|Shikoku]], each ​linked through ​sacred ​center / ‌world navel ‌/ axis ​mundi.

sources.citation: The Cambridge History of Japan, vol. 4: Early Modern Japan (Cambridge, 1991).

cultural-legacy.body: Nagoya's ​reputation is ‌food ‌first: miso-katsu, ​tebasaki ​chicken wings, ​kishimen ​flat noodles, ​and ‌the beloved ​'morning' ​custom in ‌which ​a coffee ‌order ​arrives with ‌toast, ​egg, and ​ogura ​toast. The ​Tokugawa ​Art Museum, ‌on ​the ‌castle grounds, ​holds ‌the Genji ​Monogatari ‌scrolls and ​the ‌heirlooms of ​the ​Owari house. ‌Toyota ‌Motor Corporation ‌— ​and with ​it ‌the whole ​Chūkyō ​industrial zone ‌— ​anchors an ​economy ‌that still ​supplies ‌a large ​share ​of Japan's ​exports; ​Central Japan ‌Airport ‌(Centrair), the ​2005 ‌World Exposition ​site, ​and the ‌SCMaglev ‌test line ‌through ‌the mountains ​behind ‌the city ​all ​read as ​the ‌modern ​descendants of ​the ​Tōkaidō junction ‌Ieyasu ​chose in 1610. ​The ​castle, with ‌its ​rebuilt wooden ‌palace, ​remains the ‌emblem ​— a ‌message ‌of peace ​that ​has outlasted ​every ​war it ‌was ‌built to ​prevent.[^1]

sources.citation: The Cambridge History of Japan, vol. 4: Early Modern Japan (Cambridge, 1991).

archaeology.body: The ​Honmaru Palace ‌of ‌Nagoya ​Castle survived ​in ​measured ​drawings and ​photographs ‌until ​its destruction ​in ‌1945; excavations ​of ‌its ​buried foundations ‌(2009–2010) ​allowed ​a faithful ​wooden ​reconstruction, ​opened in ‌2018 ​— one ‌of ​Japan's ‌most celebrated ​modern ‌traditional ​builds — ‌while ​the ​1959 concrete ‌keep ‌awaits its ‌own ​re-evaluation. ​Excavation at ‌Kiyosu ​Castle ​(2009) uncovered ‌the ​buried ​stone bases ‌of ​Nobunaga-era tenshu. ‌The ​city's ​older sacred ​stratum ​survives ‌at Atsuta ‌Jingū, ​the ‌great shrine ​south ​of the ‌center ‌that ‌houses the ‌Kusanagi ​sword ‌and has ​drawn ​pilgrims ​for well ‌over ​a millennium; ​the ​Tokugawa-en ‌garden preserves ​the ​Owari ​lordly residence ‌grounds. ​And ‌the castle ​town's ‌grid itself ​— ‌one ‌of Japan's ​classic ​jōkamachi ​plans — ​is ‌the ‌largest standing ​artifact.[^1]

meditation.body: Not ​every sacred ‌place begins ‌holy. ​Some become ​important ​simply by ​being where ​roads ‌meet — ​and ​Nagoya is ‌the purest ​case ‌in Japan. ​There was ‌no ​ancient shrine ​city ​here, no ​imperial capital, ​no ‌mythic island: ​a ‌plain at ​the crossroads, ‌a ​name meaning ‌'peaceful ​ancient house,' ‌and a ​shogun's ​decision to ‌build an ‌unnecessary ‌fortress. Yet ​crossroads ​accumulate meaning ‌the way ​rivers ​accumulate silt. ‌The ​castle made ​a market; ‌the ​market made ‌a merchant ​culture; ​the merchants ​made ​an industrial ‌belt; the ‌industry ​made a ‌global ​city. The ​golden shachihoko ‌swimming ‌on the ‌keep's ridge ‌beam ​are the ‌perfect ​emblem of ​the whole ​process ‌— mythical ​beasts ​pressed into ​service as ‌fire ​insurance, wonder ​made ​practical. Nagoya ‌suggests that ​holiness, ‌in the ​long run, ‌may ​be nothing ‌more ‌mysterious than ​a place ​where ​human attention ​has ‌gathered long ‌enough to ​compound.[^1]
